problem: Existing surveys on urban computing and autonomous driving are model-centric and single-domain (mostly single-vehicle terrain data), and embodied-agent work focuses on controlled indoor settings, so none of them cover how multidomain urban data (terrain, aerial, space) should be handled end to end.
motivation: Urban environments bring environmental variability, limited observability and interaction complexity, which single-domain data cannot handle. A data-centric view of the full lifecycle is needed to turn heterogeneous urban streams into actionable embodied capabilities.
key_idea: Organize the field around a four-stage multidomain Data Lifecycle (Perception, Management, Modeling, Task Application) for Urban Embodied Agents, fusing terrain, aerial and space data.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations or experiments can be cited. The survey argues that data management should move from static storage to active agent memory, and that integration strategies are needed to bridge gaps between domains. It presents this data-centric view as a route to robust urban embodied agents.
method: Data Perception: taxonomy of how UrbanEAs sense data from terrain, aerial and space domains.
Data Management: covers the evolution from static data storage to active agent memory.
Data Modeling: analyzes integration strategies to bridge gaps between multidomain data.
Task Application: reviews downstream tasks of Urban Scene QA (SQA), Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) and Human-Agent Collaboration (HAC).
Outlook: discusses the social impact of the lifecycle, open problems and future directions.

setting.observation: multidomain: terrain, aerial and space data

numbers_note: abstract only; survey paper with no experimental results
results: This is a survey with no reported quantitative results. Its contribution is a unified four-stage data lifecycle framework and a taxonomy for each stage, together with a review of SQA, VLN and HAC applications.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so the coverage and depth of the review could not be assessed.
As a survey, it offers no empirical validation of the proposed lifecycle.
